problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###  

**a. Verdict**  
I have found a complete solution. The minimum possible number of tiles is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]

**b. Method Sketch**  
1. **Permutation of uncovered squares.**  
   Let \(n=2025\).  In each row \(i\) the uncovered unit square lies in column \(p(i)\); the condition that each column also contains exactly one uncovered square forces \(p\) to be a permutation of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\).

2. **Separation into left and right parts.**  
   For row \(i\) define the *left part* \(L_i=\{(i,j):1\le j<p(i)\}\) and the *right part* \(R_i=\{(i,j):p(i)<j\le n\}\).  
   Any rectangle that meets a row must lie entirely in the left part **or** entirely in the right part of that row; otherwise it would contain the uncovered square.  Hence the left parts must be tiled by “left‑tiles’’ and the right parts by “right‑tiles’’ separately.

3. **Lower bound (Lemma 1).**  
   The lengths \(|L_i|=p(i)-1\) form the set \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\) (because \(p\) is a permutation).  Exactly one row has length \(0\); the remaining \(n-1\) rows have pairwise distinct positive lengths.  
   If a left‑tile covers the left part of a row whose length is \(L>0\), the tile must have width exactly \(L\) (it must start at column 1 and end at column \(L\)).  Such a tile cannot also cover any row whose left part has length \(L'<L\), because it would then contain a square that is uncovered in that shorter row.  Consequently each of the \(n-1\) distinct positive lengths forces a distinct left‑tile, so at least \(n-1\) left‑tiles are needed.  
   The same argument applied to the right parts (whose lengths are \(n-p(i)\) and also form \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\)) yields at least another \(n-1\) right‑tiles.  
   Therefore any admissible tiling uses at least  

   \[
   (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2
   \tag{1}
   \]

   tiles.

4. **Construction attaining the bound (Lemma 2).**  
   For each column \(j\) let \(r_j\) be the unique row with \(p(r_j)=j\) (the uncovered square in column \(j\)).  
   Place a vertical rectangle covering all squares **above** \((r_j,j)\):  

   \[
   U_j=\{(i,j):1\le i<r_j\},
   \]

   and, if \(r_j<n\), a second vertical rectangle covering all squares **below** \((r_j,j)\):  

   \[
   D_j=\{(i,j):r_j<i\le n\}.
   \]

   Each of these sets is a contiguous vertical strip, hence a legal tile.  Different columns are disjoint, and within a column the two strips are separated by the uncovered square, so the tiles are pairwise disjoint and together cover every square except the \(n\) uncovered ones.

   The column containing the uncovered square of the top row (\(r_j=1\)) contributes only its lower strip; the column containing the uncovered square of the bottom row (\(r_j=n\)) contributes only its upper strip.  All other \(n-2\) columns contribute two strips.  Hence the total number of tiles is  

   \[
   2\,(n-2)+2 = 2n-2 .
   \tag{2}
   \]

5. **Optimality.**  
   Equation (1) shows that no tiling can use fewer than \(2n-2\) tiles, while the construction above achieves exactly \(2n-2\) tiles.  Thus the bound is tight, and the minimum number of tiles equals \(2n-2\).  For \(n=2025\),

   \[
   2n-2 = 2\cdot2025-2 = 4048 .
   \]

---

**### Detailed Solution ###**  

Let  

\[
B=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i,j\le n\},\qquad n=2025 .
\]

In each row \(i\) exactly one unit square is left uncovered; denote its column by \(p(i)\).  
Because each column also contains exactly one uncovered square, the map  

\[
p:\{1,\dots ,n\}\longrightarrow\{1,\dots ,n\}
\]

is a permutation.  The set of uncovered squares is  

\[
U=\{(i,p(i))\mid i=1,\dots ,n\},
\]

and the set of squares that must be tiled is  

\[
C=B\setminus U .
\]

All tiles are axis‑parallel rectangles whose sides lie on grid lines, and no two tiles may overlap.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 1.  Separation into left and right parts  

For each row \(i\) define  

\[
L_i=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le j<p(i)\},\qquad 
R_i=\{(i,j)\mid p(i)<j\le n\}.
\]

Thus \(L_i\) is the *left part* of row \(i\) and \(R_i\) the *right part*;  

\[
C=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}L_i\;\cup\;\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}R_i ,
\qquad L_i\cap R_i=\varnothing .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Lemma 1.** *Every tile is either a left‑tile (all its squares belong to \(L_i\) for each row \(i\) it meets) or a right‑tile (all its squares belong to \(R_i\) for each row it meets).*

*Proof.*  
Assume a tile \(T\) contains a square \((i,j)\) with \(j<p(i)\) (i.e. a square of \(L_i\)).  
If \(T\) also contained a square \((i,k)\) with \(k>p(i)\) then the whole horizontal segment from column \(j\) to column \(k\) would lie inside \(T\), and in particular the uncovered square \((i,p(i))\) would be covered—a contradiction.  Hence every square of \(T\) that lies in row \(i\) must have column \(<p(i)\).  The same argument applies when \(T\) meets a square of \(R_i\).  ∎

Consequently the left parts \(\{L_i\}\) must be covered solely by left‑tiles, and the right parts solely by right‑tiles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.  Lower bound on the number of left‑tiles  

The cardinalities \(|L_i|=p(i)-1\) form the multiset \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\) because \(p\) is a permutation.  
Exactly one row (the one with \(p(i)=1\)) has \(|L_i|=0\); the remaining \(n-1\) rows have pairwise distinct positive lengths.

Order the rows so that their left‑part lengths are non‑decreasing:

\[
0=|L_{i_1}|<|L_{i_2}|<\dots<|L_{i_n}|.
\]

Consider any left‑tile \(T\).  Let \(r\) be the smallest index (in this ordered list) of a row whose left part meets \(T\).  Since all rows below \(r\) have longer left parts, the column interval of \(T\) must be exactly  

\[
\{1,2,\dots ,|L_{i_r}|\},
\]

otherwise \(T\) would either miss a square of row \(i_r\) (if its width were smaller) or would contain a square that is uncovered in some shorter row (if its width were larger).  Therefore the left part of row \(i_r\) is covered by a tile whose width equals \(|L_{i_r}|\), and this tile cannot also cover any row whose left part has a smaller length.  By induction, each distinct positive length forces a distinct left‑tile.  Hence at least \(n-1\) left‑tiles are required.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.  Lower bound on the number of right‑tiles  

The right‑part lengths are \(|R_i|=n-p(i)\); they also constitute the set \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\).  Applying the same reasoning as in the previous paragraph yields at least \(n-1\) right‑tiles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Conclusion of the lower bound.**  

Any admissible tiling uses at least  

\[
(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2
\tag{3}
\]

tiles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.  Construction achieving the bound  

For each column \(j\) let  

\[
r_j=\text{the unique row with }p(r_j)=j .
\]

Thus \((r_j,j)\) is the uncovered square in column \(j\).

Define two (possibly empty) rectangles:

* Upper strip of column \(j\):  

  \[
  U_j=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i<r_j\}.
  \]

* Lower strip of column \(j\):  

  \[
  D_j=\{(i,j)\mid r_j<i\le n\}.
  \]

If \(r_j>1\) then \(U_j\) is a vertical rectangle of height \(r_j-1\); if \(r_j<n\) then \(D_j\) is a vertical rectangle of height \(n-r_j\).  Neither rectangle contains the uncovered square \((r_j,j)\), and each consists of a contiguous set of unit squares, so it is a legal tile.

The family  

\[
\mathcal{T}= \bigl\{U_j\mid r_j>1\bigr\}\cup
            \bigl\{D_j\mid r_j<n\bigr\}
\]

covers every square of \(C\) exactly once: every covered square belongs to a unique column, and within that column it is either above or below the unique uncovered square of the column.

Counting the tiles:  

* The column whose uncovered square lies in the top row (\(r_j=1\)) contributes only its lower strip \(D_j\).  
* The column whose uncovered square lies in the bottom row (\(r_j=n\)) contributes only its upper strip \(U_j\).  
* All other \(n-2\) columns contribute both an upper and a lower strip.

Hence  

\[
|\mathcal{T}| = 2\,(n-2)+2 = 2n-2 .
\tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.  Optimality  

Equation (3) shows that no tiling can use fewer than \(2n-2\) tiles, while the construction above achieves exactly \(2n-2\) tiles.  Therefore the minimum possible number of tiles equals \(2n-2\).

For the original board with \(n=2025\),

\[
2n-2 = 2\cdot2025-2 = 4048 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Answer**  

\[
\boxed{4048}
\]
